lesson.title: The Secret Language Python Objects Speak
lesson.summary: Dunder methods are the special, double-underscore-named methods that let your own classes plug into Python's built-in syntax, like print(), len(), and the + operator, instead of only working through methods you call by name.
lesson.body:
When you call print(x) or write x + y in Python, something is happening behind the curtain. Python is not treating + as some hardcoded rule that only works on numbers and strings. Instead, it looks at the objects involved and asks each one, "do you know how to do this?" It asks by calling a specially named method on the object. Those specially named methods start and end with two underscores, like __init__ or __len__, which is why programmers call them "dunder methods," short for "double underscore." You already know one dunder method well: __init__, the method that runs automatically when you build a new object with ClassName(...). Dunder methods are that same idea, generalized: instead of only running on construction, different dunder methods run in response to different built-in operations.

This matters because it lets objects you design behave like Python's own built-in types. Without dunder methods, if you wanted a Playlist object to report how many songs it holds, you would have to write a method with some name you invent, like get_song_count(), and every caller would need to remember that specific name. With dunder methods, you can make len(playlist) just work, the same way len(my_list) or len(my_string) already does. The built-in function len() is written to look for a __len__ method on whatever you pass it, and call that. This same pattern, sometimes called operator overloading when it applies to symbols like + or ==, is what makes print(), len(), for loops, comparisons, and arithmetic all extendable to your own classes.

Here is a small, complete example.

```python
class Playlist:
    def __init__(self, songs):
        self.songs = songs

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.songs)

p = Playlist(["Blinding Lights", "Circles", "Levitating"])
print(len(p))
```

Running this prints 3. Nothing in the Playlist class defines a method literally named len, but Python's len() function does not look for a method named len, it looks for one named __len__, finds it, calls p.__len__(), and returns whatever that method returns.

You will meet many dunder methods over the next several chapters: __str__ and __repr__ control how an object displays itself, __eq__ and __lt__ control how it compares to other objects, __add__ and __mul__ control how arithmetic operators behave on it, and __iter__ and __next__ control how it behaves in a for loop. They all follow the pattern shown here: Python defines a piece of built-in syntax or a built-in function, and quietly routes it to a dunder method if your class provides one. None of this is required. A class with no dunder methods beyond __init__ works fine, it just cannot participate in built-in syntax like len(), +, or ==. Adding the right dunder method is how you opt in.
